evidence.claim: Roxbury’s scenic drive follows 3.77 miles of Route 67 and the section of Route 317 between Route 67 and Painter Hill Road.
evidence.quote: A 3.77-mile (6.07 km) section in the town of Roxbury, from the Bridgewater–Roxbury town line to 0.30 miles (0.48 km) east of Route 317, is a designated state scenic road.

evidence.claim: Roxbury’s scenic drive follows 3.77 miles of Route 67 and the section of Route 317 between Route 67 and Painter Hill Road.

evidence.claim: The road through Roxbury and Bridgewater became State Highway 125 in 1922; Route 67 followed in the 1932 renumbering.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the road from Woodbridge to Southbury (the old Oxford Turnpike) was designated as State Highway 147 and the road from Southbury to New Milford (via Roxbury and Bridgewater) was designated as State Highway 125. Route 67 was established in the 1932 state highway renumbering

evidence.claim: From the Bridgewater line, follow Route 67 into Roxbury, where it meets Route 199 and Route 317.
evidence.quote: In Roxbury, it meets the southern end of Route 199 and the western end of Route 317.

evidence.claim: The Route 67 designation continues 0.30 mile east of Route 317.

evidence.claim: The scenic branch on Route 317 heads north through the center, then northeast to Painter Hill Road, where Church Street becomes Good Hill Road.
evidence.quote: Route 317 progresses to the north along Church Street passing Roxbury Congregational Church before turning to the northeast and intersecting with Painter Hill Road, where it changes name to Good Hill Road.

evidence.quote: It was formally separated from New Milford in 1856.

evidence.quote: The center village began to take shape with the construction in 1807 of the Congregational Church

evidence.claim: Its town green was laid out in the year of incorporation.
evidence.quote: The Center Park, between Main and Center Streets, which functions as a town green, was laid in 1856 after the town's incorporation.

evidence.claim: Federal and Greek Revival buildings give the district its early nineteenth-century character; St.
evidence.quote: The architecture of the center is largely reflective of the first half of the 19th century, including Greek Revival and Federal style buildings.

evidence.claim: Mark’s Episcopal Church adds Gothic Revival architecture in wood.
evidence.quote: St. Mark's Episcopal Church, a distinctive example of Gothic Revival architecture in wood.

evidence.claim: Hat manufacturers west of the village supported its commercial life.
evidence.quote: The village benefitted economically from hat manufacturers, whose operations were to the west (further along Hat Shop Hill Road) and supported a bustling town center.

evidence.claim: More than 60 historic buildings belong to the district, including the present and former town halls.
evidence.quote: There are more than 60 historic buildings in the district

evidence.claim: More than 60 historic buildings belong to the district, including the present and former town halls.
evidence.quote: The present and former town halls are also both in the district

evidence.claim: Mine Hill’s surviving shafts record attempts to extract gold, silver and lead in the eighteenth century.
evidence.quote: a few attempts were made in the mid-18th century to extract gold, silver, and lead from the mountain.  None of these efforts lasted more than a few years, but shafts dug into the hill survive from this period.

evidence.claim: Iron mining developed after the Shepaug Spathic Iron and Steel Company bought the hill in 1865.
evidence.quote: until 1865, when the Shepaug Spathic Iron and Steel Company purchased the hill and began to develop it.

evidence.claim: A railroad carried ore down to furnaces, and a dam on Mineral Spring Brook supplied water.
evidence.quote: with a railroad carrying ore to furnaces near the base of the hill, and built a small town for the workers.  Mineral Spring Brook was dammed to create a reservoir that would provide a reliable water supply.

evidence.claim: The iron operation closed in 1905; granite quarrying continued until 1935.
evidence.quote: The iron furnace and mining operation was closed in 1905, and the stone quarry closed in 1935.

evidence.claim: Trails now reach abandoned quarries and preserved ironworks remains, with panels explaining their uses.
evidence.quote: Several miles of trails provide access to abandoned quarry areas and the preserved remains of the iron works, whose uses are explained by informational panels.

evidence.claim: The company also built a small workers’ town.
evidence.quote: built a small town for the workers.

evidence.claim: Granite from the quarry traveled by rail to New York City markets.
evidence.quote: Later in the 19th century, a granite quarry was also opened near the base of hill, its products were transported by rail to market in New York City.

evidence.claim: Roxbury Center gathers its historic buildings near the junction of Routes 67 and 317.
evidence.quote: Centered at the junction of Connecticut Routes 67 and 317

evidence.claim: The village became the community’s dominant center beginning in the 1790s, and much of its architecture dates from that period and the following 50 to 60 years.
evidence.quote: It became the dominant village in the community beginning the 1790s, and its architecture is dominated by that period and the following 50–60 years.

evidence.claim: Most district buildings stand on Weller’s Bridge Road or Church Street; Federal and Greek Revival houses predominate.
evidence.quote: Most of the buildings included in the district are on Weller's Bridge Road or Church Street, the majority of them residences in the Federal or Greek Revival style.

evidence.claim: On the town green, an obelisk marks the burial of Revolutionary War figure Seth Warner.
evidence.quote: American Revolutionary War hero Seth Warner, is buried beneath an obelisk on the town green.

evidence.claim: The district also includes the 1937 public library and a mid-nineteenth-century town hall, alongside agricultural land surrounding the village.
evidence.quote: Prominent public buildings include the Roxbury Public Library, built in 1937, the mid-19th century town hall, and two churches.

evidence.claim: alongside agricultural land surrounding the village.
evidence.quote: including land cleared for agriculture, which set the village apart from its surroundings.
